newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Tung faces juggling act on HK human rights laws.
newsitem.headline: Tung faces juggling act on HK human rights laws.

text.p: A Hong Kong member of the Beijing-appointed caucus responsible for the transition of the British colony to Chinese rule offered a hint of compromise on Monday in the row over civil liberties in the territory.

The Beijing-selected Preparatory Committee responsible for re-imposing Chinese sovereignty over Hong Kong voted on Saturday to roll back some of the territory's laws, including part of its Bill of Rights, sparking a storm of protest.
"I don't expect the chief executive and the Provisional Legislature to put in the (former) draconian laws," academic and Provisional Committee member Lau Sui-kai said on Monday.

"I expect them to ... consult the Hong Kong people, otherwise both the chief executive's prestige and the chance of re-election of many provisional legislators will be harmed or seriously damaged," he told Hong Kong radio.

The Provisional Legislature, which China will install in place of the elected chamber -- a source of considerable controversy in Hong Kong -- is expected to sit for about a year before new elections are called.
When future chief executive Tung Chee-hwa emerged from the meeting in Beijing which voted to strike down the legal clauses, he said he hoped the response in Hong Kong would not be "too emotional".
He said he would consult with Hong Kong people before proceeding, but his promises fell on deaf ears in Hong Kong's pro-democracy camp.

"Tung Chee-hwa's honeymoon with the Hong Kong people came to an abrupt end last week when he wasted no time in offering his unreserved support for the Chinese government's proposals to (water down the laws)," said politician Emily Lau on Monday.
Tung's future deputy, Anson Chan, warned that the proposals had caused concern in the United States.

"I have to say that the (decision) concerning the Bill of Rights Ordinance and repeal of legislation sent an extremely negative signal to people in America," Chan told reporters Monday night on her return from a visit to the United States.
"I clearly hope to be able to reflect the views and the feelings I have obtained on this trip to Mr Tung," she said.

Chan also noted the controversy put her in a delicate position since she is currently chief secretary of the colonial government, which opposes China on the installation of the provisional legislature and repeal of the human rights laws.
But Tung's promise of consultations raised a glimmer of hope in some quarters that he may manage to salvage a face-saving formula, the South China Morning Post said on Monday.
"His flexible and pragmatic approach to quieting the controversy is to be hailed," it said.

By refraining from simply replacing the ordinances with their older and draconian colonial versions as he had initially indicated, Tung would alleviate many fears in Hong Kong, it said. It urged him to consult all shades of opinion and draft fresh amendments acceptable to as wide a spectrum as possible.

"So it is to be hoped that by July 1 Mr Tung, after consultations with different sectors of society, will come up with new versions of the ordinances that will strike a balance between maintaining social order and preserving civil liberties," it said.
Hong Kong, a British colony for more than 150 years, reverts to China at midnight on June 30, 1997.

Many in Hong Kong fear Beijing's decision will lead to the gradual snuffing out of freedoms enjoyed in the freewheeling community of six million people, despite promises to permit their capitalist lifestyle to continue unabated for 50 years.

A telephone poll conducted by an independent watchdog, the Hong Kong Policy Viewers, after the vote on Saturday found 55 percent of 573 respondents opposed the Provisional Legislature's plan and only 17.8 percent supported the move.
